newsitem.title: GERMANY: German housing construction dips in 1996.
newsitem.headline: German housing construction dips in 1996.

text.p: The construction of new housing in Germany declined slightly in 1996, but investment levels should remain fairly steady in 1997 because of low interest rates, two German associations said on Wednesday.
The Landesbausparkassen (LBS) building society said there were 585,000 new homes built in 1996, down three percent from 603,000 in 1995. It predicted there would be 580,000 homes completed in 1997.

"The chances look quite good that the housing construction in Germany will remain at a relatively high level again in the next year," said Hartwig Hamm, director of the LBS at a news conference. "The long-term demand for housing should remain favourable."

The housing sector has been booming in Germany since the late 1980s, spurred in part by unification as well as an increase in the number of people moving to the country. The numbers of new homes built in 1995 are more than double the level of the mid-1980s.
Hamm said that the number of new homes in west Germany, which declined by nine percent to 455,000 in 1996, would fall further to about 410,000 in 1997.
In eastern Germany, where special tax breaks for construction expire at the end of 1996, the number of new housing starts should climb to 170,000 next year from 130,000 in 1996, he said.

"The relatively stable development may seem remarkable for some people," Hamm said, citing recent talk of introducing a tax on profits earned from property. "The market has so far compensated the political decisions quite well."

The Federal Association of Housing Companies (BFW), meanwhile, said the imminent expiry of a special tax break for investments in east Germany had led many investors to rush to make investments before the end of the year.
"In west Germany there was a slight upward trend in the second half after a steep drop in the first half," said Karl-Heinz Reinheimer, chairman of the BFW.

He said that investment in housing construction fell only two percent in 1996, less than earlier feared thanks to the upturn in the second half, to 192.7 billion marks from 196.6 billion marks in 1995.
